challenges.title: Ordering lunch
challenges.context: You sit down in a small café at lunchtime.

steps.speaker: maria
steps.text: Hi there! Are you ready to order?
steps.reading: HI there! are you READ-y to OR-der?
steps.translation: Hello! Do you know what you want?

choices.text: Yes, could I have the chicken sandwich, please?
choices.reading: YES, could I HAVE the CHICK-en SAND-wich, PLEASE?
choices.translation: Yes, I'd like the chicken sandwich, please.
choices.feedback: 'Could I have…, please?' is the natural, polite way to order.
choices.why: Ordering in English: 'Could I have…?', 'Can I get…?' or 'I'd like…', always with 'please'.

choices.feedback: That describes what you eat. To order, say 'Could I have the chicken sandwich?'
choices.why: Ordering is a request, not a statement. And countable nouns need 'a' or 'the': the chicken sandwich.

choices.translation: In what place is the sandwich?
choices.feedback: You're asking where it is! Just order it: 'Could I have…?'
choices.why: 'Where is…?' asks for a location. To order food, name it and add 'please'.

steps.speaker: maria
steps.text: Would you like anything to drink?
steps.reading: would you LIKE AN-y-thing to DRINK?

choices.feedback: Short, clear and polite.
choices.why: 'Just + item, please' is a natural way to order something simple.

choices.feedback: 'Like' needs an object: 'Yes, I'd like some water, please.'
choices.why: 'Would like' must be followed by something: 'I'd like a tea', 'I'd like to order'.

choices.feedback: Try a full sentence: 'No, thanks, I'm fine.'
choices.why: 'No, thanks' or 'I'm fine, thanks' politely declines an offer.

challenges.title: Lost in the neighbourhood
challenges.context: You're looking at the map on your phone. An older man stops beside you.

steps.speaker: jones
steps.text: You look a bit lost. Can I help?
steps.reading: you LOOK a bit LOST. can I HELP?
steps.translation: You seem confused about where to go. Do you need help?

choices.text: Yes, please! How do I get to the station?
choices.reading: YES, PLEASE! HOW do I GET to the STA-tion?
choices.translation: Yes! What's the way to the station?
choices.feedback: Accept the help, then ask a clear question.
choices.why: 'How do I get to…?' is the standard way to ask for directions.

choices.feedback: You admitted you're lost, then left before he could help!
choices.why: After someone offers help, ask your question: 'How do I get to…?'

choices.feedback: That doesn't answer him or ask for directions.
choices.why: 'Can I help?' is a yes/no question. Say 'Yes, please', then ask for directions.

challenges.title: Late for class
challenges.context: You rush into English class five minutes late.

steps.speaker: lee
steps.translation: You are late one more time. Why?

choices.text: Sorry I'm late. My bus was delayed.
choices.reading: SOR-ry I'm LATE. my BUS was de-LAYED.
choices.translation: I apologise. The bus came late.
choices.feedback: Apologise first, then give the reason. Very natural.
choices.why: 'Sorry I'm late' + a short reason is the classic polite apology.

choices.feedback: 'Lately' means 'recently'! You mean 'Sorry I'm late'.
choices.why: Late (not on time) ≠ lately (recently). 'I've been busy lately' = recently.

choices.feedback: 'Mate' is too casual for a teacher. Try 'Sorry I'm late'.
choices.why: Match your apology to the person: casual with friends, polite with teachers and bosses.

challenges.title: A compliment
challenges.context: Your classmate Sam notices your new jacket.

choices.text: Aw, thanks! I got it last week.
choices.reading: AW, THANKS! I GOT it LAST WEEK.
choices.translation: Thank you! I bought it last week.
choices.feedback: Accepting a compliment with thanks (and a little chat) is very natural in English.
choices.why: In English, the usual response to a compliment is simply 'Thanks!', and it's nice to add a detail.

choices.feedback: Rejecting a compliment can sound awkward in English. Just say thanks!
choices.why: Modesty is fine, but flatly disagreeing ('No, it's terrible') can make the other person feel wrong.

choices.feedback: Careful! That sounds like a declaration of love.
choices.why: 'I love your jacket' is about the jacket. 'Thanks!' is the right answer.

challenges.title: Take a photo?
challenges.context: You're at a famous bridge and want someone to take your picture.

choices.text: Excuse me, would you mind taking a photo of me?
choices.reading: ex-CUSE me, would you MIND TAK-ing a PHO-to of ME?
choices.translation: Sorry to bother you: could you take my picture?
choices.feedback: 'Would you mind + -ing?' is a very polite request. Perfect for a stranger.
choices.why: 'Would you mind…?' is one of the most polite ways to ask a favour. Note the -ing: 'mind taking'.

choices.feedback: That sounds like an order. Try 'Would you mind taking a photo of me?'
choices.why: Imperatives sound bossy to strangers. Use 'Could you…?' or 'Would you mind…?'.

choices.feedback: 'Photo' is a noun: 'take a photo of me'.
choices.why: In English we 'take a photo / a picture'. 'Photograph' can be a verb, but it's formal.

challenges.title: Small talk
challenges.context: Your neighbour Mr. Jones greets you on a sunny morning.

steps.speaker: jones
steps.translation: It's a beautiful day, don't you agree?

choices.text: Yes, it's gorgeous! Finally some sun.
choices.reading: YES, it's GOR-geous! FI-nal-ly some SUN.
choices.translation: Yes, it's beautiful! At last, a sunny day.
choices.feedback: Agree, then add a little comment. Classic British small talk!
choices.why: Questions like '…, isn't it?' invite agreement. Weather is the most common small-talk topic in the UK.

choices.feedback: Fine, but one word can end the conversation. Add a comment!
choices.why: Small talk works like a ball game: answer and add something so the other person can reply.

choices.feedback: That doesn't make sense. Agree or disagree about the weather itself.
choices.why: To agree: 'Yes, it's lovely!' To disagree politely: 'Hmm, a bit cold for me!'

challenges.title: Trying clothes
challenges.context: You're in a clothes shop. The jumper you tried on is too big.

steps.speaker: maria
steps.translation: Is the size right for you?

choices.text: It's a bit big. Do you have a smaller size?
choices.reading: it's a BIT BIG. do you HAVE a SMALL-er SIZE?
choices.translation: It's slightly too large. Is there a smaller one?
choices.feedback: A clear problem plus a polite question.
choices.why: Comparatives: big → bigger, small → smaller. 'A bit' softens the complaint.

choices.feedback: Close! Say 'too big', not 'too much big'.
choices.why: 'Too' goes straight before an adjective: too big, too small. 'Too much' goes before nouns: too much sugar.

choices.feedback: That doesn't say how it fits. Try 'It's a bit big'.
choices.why: Describe the fit with an adjective: big, small, tight, loose, or 'just right'.

challenges.title: Booking by phone
challenges.context: You call a restaurant to book a table for Friday.

steps.speaker: maria
steps.text: Good afternoon, Bella Cucina. How can I help?
steps.reading: good AF-ter-NOON, BEL-la cu-CI-na. HOW can I HELP?
steps.translation: Hello, this is the restaurant. What do you need?

choices.text: Hi, I'd like to book a table for two on Friday, please.
choices.reading: HI, I'd LIKE to BOOK a TA-ble for TWO on FRI-day, PLEASE.
choices.translation: Hello, I want to reserve a table for two people on Friday.
choices.feedback: Clear, polite and complete. Perfect for the phone.
choices.why: 'I'd like to book a table for [number] on [day]' gives the restaurant everything it needs.

choices.feedback: They'll guess, but single words sound abrupt on the phone.
choices.why: Phone English tends to be extra polite. Use full sentences with 'I'd like…'.

choices.feedback: You hung up before booking!
choices.why: Checking you've got the right place is fine, but then say what you want.

challenges.title: Oops!
challenges.context: You accidentally bump into Mr. Jones on a busy street.

choices.text: Oh, I'm so sorry! Are you OK?
choices.reading: OH, I'm SO SOR-ry! are you o-KAY?
choices.feedback: Apologise, then check on him. Kind and natural.
choices.why: 'I'm so sorry' is a strong, sincere apology. 'Are you OK?' shows you care.

choices.feedback: That's 'thank you'. After bumping into someone, apologise.
choices.why: Apologies use 'sorry'. 'Thank you' is only for thanks.

choices.feedback: That blames HIM! Say 'Sorry!' first.
choices.why: 'Watch out!' warns or blames someone. If you bumped into them, apologise.

challenges.title: Saying no nicely
challenges.context: Sam invites you out, but you have an exam tomorrow.

steps.speaker: sam
steps.text: Want to come to a party tonight?
steps.reading: WANT to COME to a PAR-ty to-NIGHT?
steps.translation: Would you like to go to a party this evening?

choices.text: Ah, I'd love to, but I've got an exam tomorrow. Next time?
choices.reading: AH, I'd LOVE to, but I've GOT an ex-AM to-MOR-row. NEXT TIME?
choices.translation: I really want to, but I have a test tomorrow. Another day?
choices.feedback: 'I'd love to, but…' softens the no, and 'Next time?' keeps things friendly.
choices.why: English often softens refusals: 'I'd love to, but…', 'Sorry, I can't tonight…', plus a suggestion.

choices.feedback: Clear, but it sounds cold (and 'want' needs 'to'). Soften it: 'I'd love to, but…'
choices.why: 'I don't want to' is grammatical but blunt. A reason and a 'maybe next time' feel kinder.

choices.feedback: 'Yes' + 'I can't' mixes yes and no.
choices.why: To accept: 'Yes, I'd love to!' To decline: 'Sorry, I can't.'

challenges.title: Hotel check-in
challenges.context: You arrive at a hotel reception.

steps.speaker: maria
steps.text: Welcome! Do you have a reservation?
steps.reading: WEL-come! do you HAVE a res-er-VA-tion?
steps.translation: Hello! Did you book a room?

choices.text: Yes, it's under the name Smith.
choices.reading: YES, it's UN-der the NAME SMITH.
choices.translation: Yes, the booking uses the name Smith.
choices.feedback: 'It's under the name…' is exactly how people check in.
choices.why: 'Under the name…' tells staff which name the booking was made with.

choices.feedback: Use the past: 'Yes, I booked a room' or 'I have a reservation'.
choices.why: The booking happened before, so use the past simple or 'I have a reservation'.

choices.feedback: Too blunt, and it needs 'a': 'Could I have a room?'
choices.why: With staff, start with 'Could I…?' or 'I'd like…'.

challenges.title: Dinner at a friend's house
challenges.context: Mr. Jones has invited you round for dinner.

steps.speaker: jones
steps.translation: The food is ready. Take as much as you want!

choices.feedback: A warm thank-you plus a compliment. Lovely.
choices.why: 'Help yourself' means 'take what you want'. Thanking the cook and complimenting the food is polite.

choices.feedback: 'Help yourself' means 'take as much food as you like', not 'help in the kitchen'!
choices.why: Some phrases aren't literal: 'Help yourself!' = please take some.

choices.feedback: You haven't eaten yet! Say 'Thank you, it looks delicious!'
choices.why: 'I'm full' is for after a meal. At the start, thank your host.

choices.text: It was delicious, thank you so much!
choices.reading: it was de-LI-cious, THANK you SO MUCH!
choices.translation: The food was very good. Thanks a lot!
choices.feedback: Past tense for a finished meal, plus warm thanks.
choices.why: The meal is finished, so use the past tense: 'It was delicious'.

choices.feedback: Kind! But the meal is over, so 'It was delicious' fits better.
choices.why: Use the past tense for something finished: was, enjoyed, loved.

choices.feedback: 'No' followed by praise is confusing!
choices.why: Start with 'Yes' when you agree: 'Yes, it was delicious!'
